strengths: Addresses a practical and largely overlooked problem: coupling of motion and dynamic exposure in video restoration, with clear physics-based motivation and well-formulated problem definition

Solid technical design combining multiple components effectively: HRBP achieves both long-range temporal modeling and parallelization, ETM provides lightweight exposure conditioning, and exposure-aware FGDF couples motion and exposure in degradation modeling

Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive SOTA comparisons across multiple method categories, strong results on new and existing benchmarks (0.62-0.73 dB gains), 5.2× speedup over recurrent methods, and good generalization to unseen GoPro and real-world videos
Valuable benchmark contributions: REDS-ME and REDS-RE provide systematic evaluation under controlled dynamic exposure conditions, addressing a gap in existing datasets
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-9, Figs. 8-13) systematically validate all major design choices including hierarchical architecture, exposure-aware modeling, and component interactions

Practical applicability: uses only standard RGB inputs (unlike event-camera methods), trains on synthetic data yet generalizes well to real-world smartphone videos with continuous exposure transitions, and decoupled degradation-restoration design improves both accuracy and efficiency
Excellent presentation: clear problem motivation, well-designed figures, comprehensive supplementary material with physics derivations, and detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty at component level: HRBP is hierarchical refinement applied to video, ETM is standard SFT layer conditioning, exposure-aware FGDF is straightforward extension of prior FGDF work. Contribution is primarily in system-level combination rather than algorithmic innovation

Synthetic dataset limitations: REDS-ME/REDS-RE use linear frame averaging which may not capture nonlinear camera sensor responses, lack other real-world factors like spatially-varying lighting and sensor noise, and provide no real-world ground truth for quantitative evaluation (only no-reference metrics on real videos)

Exposure information handling underexplored: assumes reliable exposure extraction by ETE but provides no analysis of estimation accuracy in real scenarios, Table 6 sensitivity uses perfect synthetic labels, and practical applicability limited since exposure times often unavailable from raw video

Three-stage training complexity not fully justified: complex training strategy (ETE pretraining → NetD → joint training) lacks quantitative justification, with freezing ETE justified only qualitatively. No ablation comparing to end-to-end co-optimization baseline

Limited failure analysis: no empirical exploration of failure modes with extreme out-of-plane motion or severe exposure changes, flow-based limitations acknowledged but not quantitatively assessed, and no analysis of performance boundaries

Narrow evaluation scope: only REDS-derived and GoPro datasets tested, real-world evaluation limited to smartphone videos, missing evaluation on other video restoration benchmarks or diverse camera types

Some design choices lack quantitative support: no clear justification for M=4 HRBP blocks or n=9 multi-flow pairs, saturation behavior not explored, and computational memory requirements underspecified for scalability assessment

Practical limitations acknowledged but not addressed: cannot reliably estimate exposure in real-world scenarios where metadata unavailable, and scalability to longer sequences or higher resolutions not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine limitation (dynamic exposure variation) in existing VSRDB methods
Effective and practical HRBA architecture that successfully balances long-range temporal modeling with sequence-level parallelization (5.2× speedup vs RVRT with superior accuracy)
Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablations across architectural components, exposure conditioning designs, and loss functions
Strong generalization demonstrated: state-of-the-art on REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, GoPro, and real-world videos despite synthetic-only training
Insightful visualizations and analyses: ETE embedding clustering (Fig. 7a), bidirectional kernel guidance causality (Fig. 7b), progressive feature refinement (Fig. S3)
New REDS-ME and REDS-RE benchmarks provide systematic evaluation infrastructure for VSRDB under dynamic exposure
Elegant architectural design with clear decoupling of degradation learning from restoration
Good memory efficiency compared to transformer-based alternatives (6.2 GB vs VRT's 20.5 GB)
weaknesses: Limited scope: focuses exclusively on blur-extent exposure variation; other camera factors (ISO/gain, white-balance, sensor noise, clipping) explicitly excluded, reducing practical applicability
Moderate technical novelty: individual components (hierarchical aggregation, SFT modulation, FGDF) are not novel; contribution is primarily their combination and exposure-aware application
Exposure generalization gap: ETE trained on only 5 discrete exposure levels; generalization to continuous real-world exposure relies on unvalidated interpolation assumption via ordinal structure
Limited real-world validation: only qualitative visual results on smartphone videos; no quantitative metrics or controlled experiments on real camera data beyond synthesis

Incomplete architectural justification: HRBA improvement over recurrent variant is modest (0.13 dB PSNR); why hierarchical aggregation is specifically superior over other parallelizable designs not rigorously established
Training complexity: three-stage training pipeline with frozen ETE limits adaptability; no ablation on whether fine-tuning ETE during joint training could improve results
Capacity-matched baseline insufficient: w/o ETE model only increases to 13.1M parameters vs 12.8M full model (marginal difference); harder to isolate true contribution of exposure conditioning
Optical flow dependency under severe blur not analyzed: flow estimation is challenging at 5:5 exposure levels; impact on FGDF performance and potential flow error mitigation unclear
Gap between continuous (Eq. 1) and discrete (Eq. 2) degradation formulations: approximation quality and potential information loss not quantified
Limited temporal consistency analysis: beyond tOF metric, no frame-by-frame flicker analysis or failure mode discussion for edge cases
